Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. I'm recording the 2024 PPIC October poll against the actual results. Prop 3 was polled at 67% yes and came in at 62.6%, Prop 5 was polled at 48% and came in at 45.0%, and I'm now comparing Prop 6's October numbers with its actual result.

I'm checking Prop 6's two-party share in October, which was 42.3% against an actual 46.2%. Prop 2 and Prop 4 also have their actual results noted, though their poll figures are still unclear. Given typical errors of about 4 to 5 points, I'm estimating Prop 5's chance of passing from its October two-party share of 46.4%, and noting that past polls have missed in both directions.

I'm weighing how a continuing Sept-to-Oct climb might push Prop 5 higher, though Prop 6's 2024 drop from 46 to 41 still ended at 46.2, so late movement can go either way. I'm also considering whether the strongly Democratic 2026 environment lifts a measure with mostly establishment backing, since results tend to track partisan share times each party's support.

I'm estimating the electorate's partisan split for 2026, comparing it to 2024's D+20 environment. For Prop 5, I'm working through a scenario where Democrats back it at about 62%, Republicans at 28%, and independents at 42%, which gives roughly 48% yes overall.

I'm working through how late deciders might break for Prop 5. With no campaign, voters fall back on their priors and the ballot label, and many default to "No" when the wording sounds like a process change. PPIC polls also tend to push undecided respondents toward an answer, so their unsure share is probably understated, which makes me think the measure more likely fails by a few to several points.

I'm now looking for more recent data, such as early-vote figures and other forecasts, to refine the estimate. The On Point Polling model puts Prop 5 at a 45.7% chance of passing, starting from a prior of about 70% yes based on the measure's history and its legislative origin, and then pulling down toward the polling average of 43.2%. That site may be automated, so I don't fully trust it, but its blend of prior and polls is worth noting. Its 49.5% yes figure is roughly where I'd place the measure, just under the line.

I'm now wondering whether Prop 5's 2026 poll numbers are actually in line with the rest of the record, so I want to check other sources like Emerson, Citrin Center, and CalMatters for more recent figures. I'm also weighing the On Point model's 70% prior against its polling average, since that prior looks heavy for a measure polling in the mid-40s.

I'm checking the LA Times editorial board's position on Prop 5 next.

PPIC's October 2024 poll landed close to the results in both directions: Prop 5 was polled at 48% and got 45%, while Prop 6 was polled at 41% and got 46%. Next I'll look for other Prop 5 polling and for how major editorial boards and groups lined up.

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. ### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

Lawmakers placed Proposition 5 on this year’s ballot in an attempt to change how recalls of elected officials work.

I'm checking whether results for Prop 5 are published yet, which they aren't as of the latest indexing. Since this is a forecast, I need to decide whether Yes or No is more likely to win, and the recent PPIC polling leans No, with 52% against 45% in October.

I'm going through the editorial endorsements, which are split, with some papers backing No and others backing Yes. I'm also weighing the party positions and the likely behavior of undecided voters, who have tended to break No, against the Democratic turnout edge that helps Yes but may not be enough.

I'm weighing how the No argument's point about politicians picking their own replacement compares with the Yes side's loophole argument. I'm also thinking about comparing PPIC's final polls with actual results for other California measures, where some came in a few points off the poll.

I'm pulling the 2024 and 2022 California ballot measures next, comparing their final results against the PPIC polls from before election day. My working sense is that measures polling under 50% with little campaign money usually finish under 50%, which puts the chance of a Yes win around 15 to 20 percent.

I'm weighing whether the 10-point jump in Yes support from September to October reflects partisan cues taking hold, and whether Democrats could consolidate further in the final days after Newsom's endorsement and party mailers. I'm also comparing Democratic support here against other Democratic-backed measures, where the figures ran much higher.

I'm comparing Democratic support for Prop 5 against other measures: Prop 4 drew about 60% among Democrats, while Prop 6 in 2024 likely ended with Democrats near 60 to 63% yes. Prop 5 looks weaker, so I'm estimating Democrats near 60%, independents around 42%, and Republicans around 28%, which lands the total near 47 to 48% and short of passing.

I'm checking whether Democratic support would need to climb to around 68% for Prop 5 to pass, which seems unlikely given that similar measures drew about 60% from Democrats. Republicans and independents who dislike the change could also move further toward No, and I'm weighing how Latino and older voters might split. Overall, No still looks more likely, but I want to check for any late polls around November 2-3 before settling on that.

I'm going to look for any newer polls on Prop 5 from firms like Emerson, Probolsky, Capitol Weekly, or Data for Progress, and check early-ballot return data to see who has already voted.

# Here’s what every proposition on the California ballot is about
### Prop. 5: Changes to recall process
Lawmakers placed Proposition 5 on this year’s ballot in an attempt to change how recalls of elected officials work.
This would be a California Constitutional amendment.
Currently, when a recall election takes place, voters are simultaneously asked to elect a replacement candidate.

Turnout looks set to be high at about 61%, a midterm pulling in lower-propensity voters who tend to lean "No" on ballot measures or skip them. I'm also using the PPIC party-level results to weigh how strongly D+ the electorate is.

I'm working through the expected Yes share under a few Democratic-turnout scenarios, and landing around 45 to 49 percent. A strongly Democratic electorate pushes it close to 50 but not clearly past it, so passage depends on how consolidated the Democratic vote turns out to be.

I'm weighing a possible late swing toward Yes: the poll has No at 52%, so Yes would need roughly a 4-point shift between mid-October and Election Day or a polling miss. Comparing past PPIC final polls to results, the errors run in both directions, with Prop 6 in 2024 moving about 5 points toward Yes.

The earlier figure of a 5-point gain for Prop 6 in 2024 is worth checking against this year's 45%: a similar late move would put Yes right around 50, so this is closer than the base estimate suggests.

I'm now looking at the Prop 5 numbers: September at 35 and October at 45, which averages to about 40. I'm considering whether the late upward trend could push the final result toward the October figure or a bit beyond it. I'm also weighing how PPIC's likely-voter screen handles the high-turnout, lower-propensity electorate, which skews younger and more Latino and leans Democratic.

Now I'm going back through the crosstabs at a finer level, checking the Q23 breakdown by party, gender, race, and age to see how the numbers split across groups.

I'm checking the Q23 crosstab splits, confirming the party, gender, and age groups each sum to the total, and trying to match which numbers belong to which column.

I'm reading the Q23 crosstab's second block and matching each row to a label: the first row looks like the "Don't know" share, the second like "No," and the third possibly "Yes." I'm checking that the paired counts in each demographic split sum to the column totals before I trust which row is which.

I'm checking the Children-in-household split: the parent column (n=158) shows about 67% No and 30% Yes, while the non-parent column (n=917) shows roughly 49% No and 47% Yes. Weighting those two groups back together reproduces the overall 52% No and 45% Yes, so the column reading holds up.

I'm checking whether the column order in the crosstab is reversed, since the first pair of numbers would otherwise imply Democratic-held seats are more likely to vote No, which doesn't fit with Republicans being around 28% Yes.

I'm going back over the Q23 crosstab's column order, since the labels and the data rows may not line up in the same sequence. The n-row sums give me the groups, but I need to confirm which column is which before I trust the percentages.

I'm checking the region and party counts against the total, and they fit: the regions sum to 980, the ideology groups to 1,070, and the party groups to 1,054. Democrats are about half the sample at 534, which lines up with the overall figure, so I'm reading this block's column layout as correct. I'm also wondering whether the sample is weighted so that the Los Angeles share of 245 is close to its expected share of likely voters.

I'm matching the column counts in the first crosstab block to their labels: the region counts run from 229 down to 115, the ideology counts add up to 1,070, and the party counts sum to 1,054. The order in the label text doesn't match the data order, though the order within each group does.

I'm checking how the labels in the crosstab text line up with the data rows: the label text lists the groups in reverse order, party, then ideology, then region, while the numbers run region, ideology, party. Within each group the order matches, so I'm treating the column mapping as consistent.

I'm lining up the group labels against the data order in the second crosstab block: the text lists Children, Age, Race, Gender, then Dem-Rep seat, which is the reverse of how the numbers seem to be arranged. I'm checking whether the same reversal I found in the first block applies here, with the within-group order staying the same.

I'm mapping the n-row values in the second crosstab against the group labels, working out whether the column order runs in reverse across groups the way it did in the first block. I'm starting from the Dem-Rep seat counts, where the first value is 197 and the last is 878.

I'm sorting out the Q23 crosstab's column layout: the pairs (197, 878), (158, 917), and (530, 545) each sum to 1,075, and the triples (280, 552, 243) also sum to the total. I'm working out which groups those pairs and triples belong to, starting from the positions of the first few values.

I'm trying to work out which column order the crosstab uses: the first group pairs (197, 878) and the triples don't line up with the labels if read in the same order. I'm considering whether the data runs in the reverse of the label sequence, with each group's internal order kept the same.

I'm checking whether the second block's data order runs in reverse of its group labels, the way the first one did. If so, the Dem-Rep seat pair (197, 878) would come first, then race, age, gender, and children, and the within-group ordering would stay the same.

I'm working out the column order in the second crosstab block: the first pair (197, 878) would be the Republican and Democratic seat counts, and the remaining triples and pairs would follow the other groups. I still need to pin down the within-group order before I assign the age and gender labels.

I'm trying to match the label text's group order to the data's column layout. The label text lists the party, gender, and race categories in one sequence, and the n-row pairs and triples suggest the data runs in a different group order. I'm checking whether "Other" belongs to the gender group or the race group before assigning the remaining counts.

I'm now weighing whether "Other" sits under gender or race, since the label text puts it right after Female and Male but the layout pattern suggests it may belong to the race group with Whites and Latinos.

I'm settling the mapping now: the Dem-Rep seat pair is Republican 197 and Democratic 878, and the race group should be Whites, Latinos, and Other, with Other taken as the last of the three rather than the first.

I'm trying to work out whether the race counts in block 2 follow the same order as their labels, since 680 for Whites can't be the Other category. I'm also considering whether reversing the order within each group would fix it, but Whites is clearly the largest count, so that doesn't fit either. The exact within-group order isn't essential, so I'll leave it and look at the age and other breakdowns instead.

I'm wondering how the PPIC results break down by age group, though the regional split is the main thing I have. Next I'm looking at the California Democratic Party's endorsement document to see whether it lists a position on Prop 5, since a news piece says it backs the measure. The official voter guide also matters: it shows no submitted supporter or opponent statements, so readers would only see the title and summary.

I'm looking at what a Yes vote would mean for voters, since the measure would take away their power to pick a replacement, and that framing is getting a lot of attention. Several major papers across the state, including Southern California's newspaper group, have come out against it, which points to a heavy No presence in that region.

I'm weighing the Prop 5 outcome, noting that major newspapers across the state, including Southern California's group, have come out against it while only a few McClatchy papers back it. The "Yes" side appears to have almost no active campaign, so I'm estimating its chance of winning at around 15%, which points toward "no."

I'm wondering whether the current date is past the election, so I'll try the AP or KCRA results pages to see if any counts have come in.

content.text: Early-ballot returns lean heavily Democratic, and turnout is running well ahead of 2022, which helps Yes somewhat. I'll check whether any live results pages have updated.

California voters will decide on whether the state's recall election process will change.
Proposition 5 could make removing an elected official from office as simple as answering one ballot question. Currently, a recall requires voters to decide whether or not a politician should be removed, then answer who should replace them. If passed, Prop 5 would remove the current second section, which would mean voters would be asked to elect a sucessor in a separate process.

I'm noting that early ballot returns skew Democratic at roughly 51-57%, with Republicans around 28% and others at 15-21%. Turnout looks set to be high at about 61%, a midterm pulling in lower-propensity voters who tend to lean "No" on ballot measures or skip them. I'm also using the PPIC party-level results to weigh how strongly D+ the electorate is.

I'm working through the expected Yes share under a few Democratic-turnout scenarios, and landing around 45 to 49 percent. A strongly Democratic electorate pushes it close to 50 but not clearly past it, so passage depends on how consolidated the Democratic vote turns out to be.

I'm weighing a possible late swing toward Yes: the poll has No at 52%, so Yes would need roughly a 4-point shift between mid-October and Election Day or a polling miss. Comparing past PPIC final polls to results, the errors run in both directions, with Prop 6 in 2024 moving about 5 points toward Yes.

The earlier figure of a 5-point gain for Prop 6 in 2024 is worth checking against this year's 45%: a similar late move would put Yes right around 50, so this is closer than the base estimate suggests.

I'm now looking at the Prop 5 numbers: September at 35 and October at 45, which averages to about 40. I'm considering whether the late upward trend could push the final result toward the October figure or a bit beyond it. I'm also weighing how PPIC's likely-voter screen handles the high-turnout, lower-propensity electorate, which skews younger and more Latino and leans Democratic.

Now I'm going back through the crosstabs at a finer level, checking the Q23 breakdown by party, gender, race, and age to see how the numbers split across groups.

I'm checking the Q23 crosstab splits, confirming the party, gender, and age groups each sum to the total, and trying to match which numbers belong to which column.

I'm reading the Q23 crosstab's second block and matching each row to a label: the first row looks like the "Don't know" share, the second like "No," and the third possibly "Yes." I'm checking that the paired counts in each demographic split sum to the column totals before I trust which row is which.

I'm checking the Children-in-household split: the parent column (n=158) shows about 67% No and 30% Yes, while the non-parent column (n=917) shows roughly 49% No and 47% Yes. Weighting those two groups back together reproduces the overall 52% No and 45% Yes, so the column reading holds up.

I'm checking whether the column order in the crosstab is reversed, since the first pair of numbers would otherwise imply Democratic-held seats are more likely to vote No, which doesn't fit with Republicans being around 28% Yes.

I'm going back over the Q23 crosstab's column order, since the labels and the data rows may not line up in the same sequence. The n-row sums give me the groups, but I need to confirm which column is which before I trust the percentages.

I'm checking the region and party counts against the total, and they fit: the regions sum to 980, the ideology groups to 1,070, and the party groups to 1,054. Democrats are about half the sample at 534, which lines up with the overall figure, so I'm reading this block's column layout as correct. I'm also wondering whether the sample is weighted so that the Los Angeles share of 245 is close to its expected share of likely voters.

I'm matching the column counts in the first crosstab block to their labels: the region counts run from 229 down to 115, the ideology counts add up to 1,070, and the party counts sum to 1,054. The order in the label text doesn't match the data order, though the order within each group does.

I'm checking how the labels in the crosstab text line up with the data rows: the label text lists the groups in reverse order, party, then ideology, then region, while the numbers run region, ideology, party. Within each group the order matches, so I'm treating the column mapping as consistent.

I'm lining up the group labels against the data order in the second crosstab block: the text lists Children, Age, Race, Gender, then Dem-Rep seat, which is the reverse of how the numbers seem to be arranged. I'm checking whether the same reversal I found in the first block applies here, with the within-group order staying the same.

I'm mapping the n-row values in the second crosstab against the group labels, working out whether the column order runs in reverse across groups the way it did in the first block. I'm starting from the Dem-Rep seat counts, where the first value is 197 and the last is 878.

I'm sorting out the Q23 crosstab's column layout: the pairs (197, 878), (158, 917), and (530, 545) each sum to 1,075, and the triples (280, 552, 243) also sum to the total. I'm working out which groups those pairs and triples belong to, starting from the positions of the first few values.

I'm trying to work out which column order the crosstab uses: the first group pairs (197, 878) and the triples don't line up with the labels if read in the same order. I'm considering whether the data runs in the reverse of the label sequence, with each group's internal order kept the same.

I'm checking whether the second block's data order runs in reverse of its group labels, the way the first one did. If so, the Dem-Rep seat pair (197, 878) would come first, then race, age, gender, and children, and the within-group ordering would stay the same.

I'm working out the column order in the second crosstab block: the first pair (197, 878) would be the Republican and Democratic seat counts, and the remaining triples and pairs would follow the other groups. I still need to pin down the within-group order before I assign the age and gender labels.

I'm trying to match the label text's group order to the data's column layout. The label text lists the party, gender, and race categories in one sequence, and the n-row pairs and triples suggest the data runs in a different group order. I'm checking whether "Other" belongs to the gender group or the race group before assigning the remaining counts.

I'm now weighing whether "Other" sits under gender or race, since the label text puts it right after Female and Male but the layout pattern suggests it may belong to the race group with Whites and Latinos.

I'm settling the mapping now: the Dem-Rep seat pair is Republican 197 and Democratic 878, and the race group should be Whites, Latinos, and Other, with Other taken as the last of the three rather than the first.

I'm trying to work out whether the race counts in block 2 follow the same order as their labels, since 680 for Whites can't be the Other category. I'm also considering whether reversing the order within each group would fix it, but Whites is clearly the largest count, so that doesn't fit either. The exact within-group order isn't essential, so I'll leave it and look at the age and other breakdowns instead.

I'm wondering how the PPIC results break down by age group, though the regional split is the main thing I have. Next I'm looking at the California Democratic Party's endorsement document to see whether it lists a position on Prop 5, since a news piece says it backs the measure. The official voter guide also matters: it shows no submitted supporter or opponent statements, so readers would only see the title and summary.

I'm looking at what a Yes vote would mean for voters, since the measure would take away their power to pick a replacement, and that framing is getting a lot of attention. Several major papers across the state, including Southern California's newspaper group, have come out against it, which points to a heavy No presence in that region.

I'm weighing the Prop 5 outcome, noting that major newspapers across the state, including Southern California's group, have come out against it while only a few McClatchy papers back it. The "Yes" side appears to have almost no active campaign, so I'm estimating its chance of winning at around 15%, which points toward "no."

I'm wondering whether the current date is past the election, so I'll try the AP or KCRA results pages to see if any counts have come in.

California’s Democratic and Republican party organizations have issued competing road maps for the Nov. 3 general election, endorsing opposing slates for statewide office and taking sharply different positions on many of the 14 propositions before voters.
The recommendations are party endorsements, not official voting instructions.
Voters may support any candidate or position regardless of registration, and the state parties generally leave city, county and other local contests to local party committees.

The California Democratic Party endorsed Xavier Becerra for governor and Fiona Ma for lieutenant governor.

For the Board of Equalization, Democrats endorsed Nelson Esparza in District 1, Sally Lieber in District 2, Mike Gipson in District 3 and Tom Umberg in District 4.
In contests affecting the Mariposa area, the party endorsed Michael Masuda in the 5th Congressional District and Jaron Brandon in the 4th State Senate District.

Voters may support any candidate or position regardless of registration, and the state parties generally leave city, county and other local contests to local party committees.
## Democratic Party recommendations
The California Democratic Party endorsed Xavier Becerra for governor and Fiona Ma for lieutenant governor.
Its statewide slate also includes Secretary of State Shirley Weber, Controller Malia Cohen, Treasurer Eleni Kounalakis, Attorney General Rob Bonta, Insurance Commissioner Ben Allen and Superintendent of Public Instruction Richard Barrera.
For the Board of Equalization, Democrats endorsed Nelson Esparza in District 1, Sally Lieber in District 2, Mike Gipson in District 3 and Tom Umberg in District 4.
In contests affecting the Mariposa area, the party endorsed Michael Masuda in the 5th Congressional District and Jaron Brandon in the 4th State Senate District.
The party’s published statewide list does not show an endorsement in the 8th Assembly District.
On the statewide measures, the Democratic Party recommends “yes” votes on Propositions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 37, 38

Plugging in rough turnout weights, the total lands close to 50%, so it's borderline. Looking at how similar Democratic-backed measures have done in California, I need to judge whether Dem consolidation would push the number higher.

I'm comparing the last PPIC poll numbers against past outcomes for similar measures, to see how much support typically shifts between the October survey and election day. Prop 6 gained about five points late, while Prop 5 in 2024 and Prop 3 both dropped, so I'm gathering more examples from recent elections to get a steadier estimate.

I'm pulling together the PPIC October poll numbers against the actual results for recent measures, to see how far support typically moves before election day. Prop 3 and Prop 5 dropped a few points, while Prop 6 gained about five, so I'm checking the earlier years too.

I'm tallying the PPIC October poll numbers against final results for more recent measures. Prop 30 seems to have dropped sharply, while Prop 31 and Prop 16 gained several points, so the late movement clearly varies a lot from measure to measure.

I'm working out the error margin for PPIC's final poll, which averages about 3.5 points with a spread near 4. For Prop 5 I need roughly a 3.5-point gain to reach 48.5%, and the estimated chance of that depends on whether the poll error is centered at zero, slightly positive, or slightly negative. I'm also weighing whether a Democratic-leaning electorate in 2024 might have pushed Dem-backed measures in a systematic direction.

I'm checking how the PPIC sample's Democratic lean compares with the likely actual electorate, since a Dem-heavier sample would overstate Yes on a party-aligned measure. The early-return splits look similar to the sample's composition, so that gap may be small.

I'm weighing a few more points in favor of Yes: the ballot wording is the official one, so it matches what voters will see. The Democratic slate card's framing could pull low-information Democrats toward Yes, possibly lifting their share to around 65-70%. The catch is whether Republican support for Prop 5 would be as high as I'm assuming, so I'm checking that next.

I'm weighing whether partisan consolidation could push the final number up toward 47%. Looking at how other Democratic-backed measures moved from the September to October PPIC polls, most gained three to ten points, and Prop 5 gained the most at about ten. If that party-cue movement continues through the final ten days, another two or three points seems plausible.

I'm estimating the chance that Yes clears 50% at roughly 40%, a sizable share, and I'm weighing whether late voters, who likely lean on slate mailers arriving in the final two weeks, would push the number up further.

I'm checking whether anything else might push the Yes share past the threshold. Right now, a recall election asks Californians two questions at once.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Support

Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

Right now, a recall election asks Californians two questions at once.
The second one is the problem: it hands the seat to whoever finishes first in a crowded field, sometimes with a sliver of the vote, and it locks the recalled official out of the race entirely.

Proposition 5 puts the decision back where it belongs.
Recall an official, and the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run and voters choose a replacement outright. This isn’t about protecting any party or any officeholder. It’s about making sure the person who ends up in the seat actually won it.

I'm weighing the case for Yes once more, with the reform-minded and "majority rule" framing, and the Prop 50 comparison I'd rather not chase. I'm looking at the prediction market data for Prop 5, the recall elections measure, which has a 32% chance to pass across Kalshi and Polymarket. The markets are thin, but they lean toward No, so the signals point the same way. I'm now weighing whether to d

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the single-word framing points to the No side. Still, I want to check whether the Yes side could win, starting with the Democratic-leaning electorate and the "majority rule" argument for the recall replacement.

I'm weighing the case for Yes once more, with the reform-minded and "majority rule" framing, and the Prop 50 comparison I'd rather not chase. I'm now looking at the expected final composition of the electorate: Democrats around half of voters, Republicans near a quarter to a third, and late-deciding nonpartisan voters likely pushing their share higher. I want to pin down what Democratic voters are likely to do before settling on the estimate.

I'm working through the expected final vote split by party: Democrats around 60% Yes, Republicans around 25%, and nonpartisan voters around 41%. Weighting those by the rough electorate shares gives an overall Yes figure of about 46%, leaving No near 54%. I'm also estimating the uncertainty, which comes mostly from the Democratic share.

I'm running the numbers on the Yes side: a combined standard deviation of about 3.9 points around a 46% expected share, which puts the chance of Yes clearing 50% at roughly 17%. I'm now checking how much that changes if Democratic support ends up closer to 64%.

Checking the 2024 Prop 6 party breakdown next, to see whether Democrats consolidated more by the final result than the October polls showed.

I'm checking the 2024 Prop 6 partisan breakdown to see how far Democrats consolidated between the October polls and the final result, which should help calibrate the likely Democratic share this time. I'm planning to pull the PPIC crosstabs and look for the offset near the Prop 6 question.

Prediction markets lean No at about 22% on Kalshi and 41% on Polymarket. To gauge how far Democrats might consolidate, I'm comparing with the 2024 Prop 6 case, which polled 41% in October and finished at 46.2%.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm trying to calibrate against the October 2024 PPIC crosstabs for Prop 6, and I need to get the row order right: the "don't know" figures come first, then the No and Yes shares.

I'm reading the October PPIC table row by row: the No share comes out at 56% overall, and Yes at 41%. Looking at the Yes row by group, Democrats are at 56%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 38%.

I'm working out the implied electorate weights for the 2024 Prop 6 result: if Democrats came in around 65%, Republicans near 22%, and independents at 42%, the weighted total lands close to the actual 46.2% yes. I'm then carrying those same shifts over to Prop 5 for 2026 and getting a rough final figure near 50%.

I'm weighing the October PPIC figures against the September poll for Prop 6, where it stood at 46% yes versus 41% in October. Taking the September number as the more representative one, the final 46.2% fits it closely, which suggests the October reading was just noise. Averaging the two polls gives about 43.5%, and the actual result landed roughly 2.7 points above that. For Prop 5 in 2026 I'm noting the September figure at 35% and the October figure at 45%.

I'm weighing whether the October reading was just a noisy high, which would put Prop 5's final near 44%, or whether the rise reflects a real trend that could carry it to 47-49%. Other propositions in the same series also moved up between September and October, and Prop 5's jump is the largest of them, so I'm checking the September party splits for Prop 5 next.

The October jump for Democrats, from 40 to 56, looks like cue-taking after the party's endorsement and the slate mailers. Republicans moved the other way, from 34 down to 28. I'm checking whether earlier low-information measures in prior elections showed similar late swings, starting with how Prop 6 moved in 2024.

I'm checking the 2024 Prop 5 figures from the same crosstabs next: the Democratic Yes share looks like it came in around 68%, and I want to confirm that against the other rows before comparing it to the October reading.

I'm checking the Prop 5 Yes row from the October 2024 table, where Democrats come in at 68%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 43%, for an overall total of 48% against the actual 45%. That suggests the Democratic share in that poll ran high relative to the final result, so I'm guessing Prop 6's Democratic figure could have shifted up as well.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024: both Democratic-backed measures finished near 45-46% despite polls showing 48 and 41. That suggests the final Yes share for a similar 2026 measure would land around 47-48%, and getting past 50% would need unusually strong consolidation.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024 against the broader electorate: both Democratic-backed measures landed in the mid-40s despite polling higher, so I'm reconsidering whether the Democratic environment in 2026 really adds enough to push a low-salience measure past 50%.

I'm checking the 2026 Prop 5 electorate estimate: the Dem-margin figure is around D+22 to D+25, and I'm running a rough regression off the 2024 Prop 5 and Prop 6 results, which both landed near 45-46%. Projecting that forward gives a final around 46-47%, so I'd put the chance of Yes clearing 50% at roughly 15-20%.

I'm weighing whether the Democratic slate language, which frames the measure as protecting the right to recall, would hold up as well as the 2024 "slavery" wording did, since that one still lost with Democrats and independents peeling off over the confusion. Overall I'd lean toward the lower-salience, GOP-opposed pattern holding, so Yes staying under 50% still looks like the more likely outcome.

Next I want to confirm the outcome isn't already known by checking for early returns on the Prop 5 recall, since the latest coverage I've seen stops at Nov 2.

I'm going to search for the Prop 5 results and election night race calls, to see whether the outcome is already reported.

I'm trying to calibrate against the October 2024 PPIC crosstabs for Prop 6, and I need to get the row order right: the "don't know" figures come first, then the No and Yes shares.

I'm reading the October PPIC table row by row: the No share comes out at 56% overall, and Yes at 41%. Looking at the Yes row by group, Democrats are at 56%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 38%.

I'm working out the implied electorate weights for the 2024 Prop 6 result: if Democrats came in around 65%, Republicans near 22%, and independents at 42%, the weighted total lands close to the actual 46.2% yes. I'm then carrying those same shifts over to Prop 5 for 2026 and getting a rough final figure near 50%.

I'm weighing the October PPIC figures against the September poll for Prop 6, where it stood at 46% yes versus 41% in October. Taking the September number as the more representative one, the final 46.2% fits it closely, which suggests the October reading was just noise. Averaging the two polls gives about 43.5%, and the actual result landed roughly 2.7 points above that. For Prop 5 in 2026 I'm noting the September figure at 35% and the October figure at 45%.

I'm weighing whether the October reading was just a noisy high, which would put Prop 5's final near 44%, or whether the rise reflects a real trend that could carry it to 47-49%. Other propositions in the same series also moved up between September and October, and Prop 5's jump is the largest of them, so I'm checking the September party splits for Prop 5 next.

The October jump for Democrats, from 40 to 56, looks like cue-taking after the party's endorsement and the slate mailers. Republicans moved the other way, from 34 down to 28. I'm checking whether earlier low-information measures in prior elections showed similar late swings, starting with how Prop 6 moved in 2024.

I'm checking the 2024 Prop 5 figures from the same crosstabs next: the Democratic Yes share looks like it came in around 68%, and I want to confirm that against the other rows before comparing it to the October reading.

I'm checking the Prop 5 Yes row from the October 2024 table, where Democrats come in at 68%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 43%, for an overall total of 48% against the actual 45%. That suggests the Democratic share in that poll ran high relative to the final result, so I'm guessing Prop 6's Democratic figure could have shifted up as well.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024: both Democratic-backed measures finished near 45-46% despite polls showing 48 and 41. That suggests the final Yes share for a similar 2026 measure would land around 47-48%, and getting past 50% would need unusually strong consolidation.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024 against the broader electorate: both Democratic-backed measures landed in the mid-40s despite polling higher, so I'm reconsidering whether the Democratic environment in 2026 really adds enough to push a low-salience measure past 50%.

I'm checking the 2026 Prop 5 electorate estimate: the Dem-margin figure is around D+22 to D+25, and I'm running a rough regression off the 2024 Prop 5 and Prop 6 results, which both landed near 45-46%. Projecting that forward gives a final around 46-47%, so I'd put the chance of Yes clearing 50% at roughly 15-20%.

I'm weighing whether the Democratic slate language, which frames the measure as protecting the right to recall, would hold up as well as the 2024 "slavery" wording did, since that one still lost with Democrats and independents peeling off over the confusion. Overall I'd lean toward the lower-salience, GOP-opposed pattern holding, so Yes staying under 50% still looks like the more likely outcome.

Next I want to confirm the outcome isn't already known by checking for early returns on the Prop 5 recall, since the latest coverage I've seen stops at Nov 2.

I'm going to search for the Prop 5 results and election night race calls, to see whether the outcome is already reported.

The 2024 Prop 6 had nearly the same party split as Prop 5 now, and it finished at 46.2%, so Democratic-backed low-salience amendments have tended to land in the mid-40s. I'm running one last check for any election-night results.

5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

Results are reported as soon as they are available. AP’s Decision Team declares winners (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-we-declare-winners/) when certain the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory. Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Next I'm weighing the historical record: recall-related measures and legislature-placed amendments have had mixed results, and this one takes away voters' say in choosing a replacement, which tends to make them wary. Since it was placed by Democrats after the 2021 recall, it's been coded along partisan lines, and I'm checking the crosstabs and any other polls to see how firm that Democratic support really is at 56% yes.

I'm going to look into the newspaper endorsements and how CalMatters explains the measure, then check who is funding it and whether any organized opposition exists, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association or the California Republican Party. I also want to see whether the results page on the Secretary of State site has anything posted yet, since the date may be later than what I've assumed.

California voters will decide in November whether to overhaul the state's recall election process. Proposition 5, authored by former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman, would change how California fills vacancies when state officials are recalled. ***Two Questions in Recall Elections.*** In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office.

If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.

The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.

If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
