California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures
By WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and NICOLE NORMAN (https://www.politico.com/staff/nicole-norman)
10/05/2026 03:09 PM EDT
State Sen. Josh Newman talks during a Senate session in Sacramento, California, on June 11, 2018. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.
Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.
All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.
“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser , a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”
The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom , triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder (https://www.politico.com/news/2021/08/17/ca-recall-election-larry-elder-505735) — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/09/15/california-elections-chief-wants-recall-overhaul-possibly-as-soon-as-2022-1391082), and election committees revved up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2021/09/16/with-newsom-secure-democrats-look-to-restrain-recall-494353).
But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.
A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.
Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.
But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).
Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.
Assemblymember Alex Lee , one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.
“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.
Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”
Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.
“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#65120806060417110d1c25150a090c110c060a4b060a08) .
TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.
2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson ’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan , the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317427465.html) to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio ’s Reform California organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730). The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.
4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge (https://x.com/CAgovernor/status/2105470383281598682) with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.
5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.” (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/03/bernie-sanders-billionaire-tax-san-francisco-rally-01105995)
6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/events/barbeque-beer-ballots-ramona-10-05-2026) today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?utm_source=firefox-newtab-en-us), DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.
7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM). The second warns people (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EbT1lgt8ic4) of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.
IN OTHER NEWS
HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel , the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family (https://miriampawel.com/the-browns-of-california/) and Cesar Chavez (https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/27/books/review/the-crusades-of-cesar-chavez-by-miriam-pawel.html), for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear (https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/10/08/i-taste-ashes-in-the-wind-nuclear-weapons-jerry-brown/) disarmament. Register here (https://libraryca.libcal.com/event/17654368) .
THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/05/democrats-smp-attack-ads-epstein-01106408).
Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.
And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

Then-gubernatorial candidate Arnold Schwarzenegger celebrates his victory in the California recall election with his wife Maria Shriver at the Century Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles, on Oct. 7, 2003.
Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process.
Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Vot

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. I'm weighing what's known about Prop 5: as of October 5 there was no organized financial backing to pass it, though local outlets mention small campaign efforts on both sides. Newman sounds not optimistic, and the PPIC October poll has it at 45 to 52. I'm now looking at a later Berkeley IGS poll.

I'm checking whether the Berkeley IGS poll also covered Prop 5, since the Politico piece only mentions Prop 4 there. A California Today note says no independent poll had published a Prop 5 result as of October 12, so I'm looking at other pollsters to see if any did.

I'm working through the historical PPIC numbers and noticing that the 45-52 October figure is a shift of about ten points for Yes from September. A move like that often reflects partisans lining up behind party endorsements, and if Democrats break strongly yes while Republicans and independents lean no, the overall tally could still come in below half, though it's close enough to watch.

I'm now planning to pin down the PPIC crosstab sample sizes for likely voters by party, since the party mix determines whether the 45-52 split could tighten toward a majority.

I'm checking the PPIC crosstabs against the headline numbers: Becerra leads Hilton 61 to 37, which points to an electorate leaning heavily Democratic. Working through the party split, Democrats at 56% yes, Republicans at 28%, and independents at 40% gives roughly 44 to 45% overall, so the topline holds together. I'm also estimating what it would take to reach a majority, something like Democrats near 68%, Republicans around 30%, and independents near 45%.

I'm now weighing whether Democratic voter-guide endorsements and party cues could push Democratic support for Prop 5 up another five to ten points by Election Day, given how much it already jumped from September to October. Some of that jump may just be sampling noise, since subgroups of around 250 carry a margin of about six points, but cue-taking among lower-information voters is probably part of it too.

I'm recalling the recent California measures that failed with similar margins, like the 2024 involuntary servitude amendment and the bond measure that lost 45 to 55. With no organized opposition and little spending, I expect voters will lean on the ballot label and the official arguments in the voter guide.

I'm going back over earlier California ballot measures that were placed by the Legislature, like the 2020 affirmative action amendment that failed and the parolee voting measure that passed, to see how voters have treated similar items.

I'm recalling how California's legislatively placed amendments have fared, like the 2005 Props 76 and 77 that failed, while the 2010 top-two primary and 2012 term-limits measures passed. Measures that restrict how the electoral process works tend to struggle, and the 2003 recall gives a sense of voters wanting a say over who replaces an officer. For Prop 5, which would have the governor appoint replacements for statewide officers other than himself, I'm weighing whether that same instinct cuts against it.

I'm checking whether a Democratic turnout surge could push the Yes side above half, since the likely-voter sample leans heavily Democratic with Becerra up 61 to 37. Recalling recent California results, Newsom and Biden-era margins suggest the electorate could tilt further blue than the poll assumes.

I'm comparing this to 2022, when Prop 1 on abortion passed with about 67%, but I don't think partisanship drives Prop 5 nearly as strongly. I'm also reading the ballot label, which says the measure would fill recall vacancies by special election or appointment instead of the replacement vote on the recall ballot, with the fiscal effect unknown.

I'm wondering whether other polls, like Berkeley IGS or Emerson, have measured Prop 5, and I'm checking how the No side is funded and whether the Republican Party or a taxpayer group has taken a position.

I'm checking whether the Republican Party, a taxpayer group, or any other organization has taken a position or funded the No side, and I'm also looking for newspaper editorial endorsements from major California outlets.

### Summary
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026
Link copied!

California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

Proposition 5 rewrites three sections of the California Constitution
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article II, sections 15 and 17, and Article V, section 10. It changes no statute directly. Its edits are short:
Section 15(a) strikes the words "and, if appropriate, to elect a successor" from the description of a recall election, leaving an election "to determine whether to recall an officer."
Section 15(c) strikes the sentence that makes "the candidate who receives a plurality" the successor, and strikes the ban on the targeted officer being a candidate. In their place it provides that if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
Article V, section 10(b) is new. If the Governor is removed by recall, "the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term," unless the recall comes "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term." In that case "a special election shall be called to replace the Governor," consolidated with the statewide primary; a candidate with a majority at the primary takes office, and otherwise "the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election."
Section 17 moves the job of running a governor's recall from the lieutenant governor, who would now be the successor, to the secretary of state, with the controller taking over if the governor and secretary of state are targeted at the same time.
The Attorney General's ballot label calls it a change for "statewide officers," but the text applies to every state officer subject to recall, and the LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) describes its effect on Senate and Assembly seats as well. Prop 5 does not change how a recall qualifies, how quickly the election is held, or how local recalls work.
California recall law today: 12% of the last vote, two questions, a plurality winner
The power to recall is in Article II (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2014.&article=II) of the Constitution: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." A recall of a statewide officer needs signatures equal to 12% of the last vote for the office, including 1% of the last vote in each of five counties; senators, Assembly members, Board of Equalization members and appellate and trial judges need 20%. Proponents have 160 days to gather them, and the "sufficiency of reason is not reviewable." Once signatures are certified, the election is held 60 to 80 days later, or within 180 days to coincide with a regular election. An officer who survives is reimbursed for recall expenses, and no new recall can begin for six months.
The successor rule sits in section 15(c), last amended by Proposition 183 in 1994: if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate." Elections Code section 11385 repeats it: the candidate "receiving the highest number of votes for the office shall be declared elected for the unexpired term."
Prop 5 would replace that with the rules California already uses when an office falls vacant for any other reason. The lieutenant governor becomes governor under Article V, section 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=V). For the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction and Board of Equalization, Article V, section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=V) has the governor nominate a replacement who takes office on confirmation by a majority of each house, or automatically if neither house acts within 90 days. For a legislative seat, Elections Code section 10703 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=10703) requires a special election "at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days" after the governor's proclamation, which must be issued within 14 days of the vacancy.
California has already made this change for local officials. Since January 1, 2023, under AB 2582 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2582), recalls of local officers have asked only whether to remove the officer; under Elections Code section 11382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=11382) the office "shall be vacant until it is filled according to law," and the recalled officer may not be appointed to the vacancy. Prop 5 uses the same structure and much of the same wording for state offices, which only a constitutional amendment can reach.
California recall elections are keeping their signature thresholds and timelines under Proposition 5 while the replacement question gives way to succession, appointment and special elections, as the measure's text and the California Constitution show in October 2026. The governor's seat under Prop 5: The lieutenant governor, then possibly a special election
For a recalled governor, Prop 5 creates a two-track rule keyed to timing. Late in a term, the lieutenant governor serves out the remainder, and no election is held for the seat until the next regular gubernatorial election. Early in a term, before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election during the governor's first two years, the lieutenant governor takes over and a special election is held alongside the next statewide primary. A majority winner there serves the rest of the term; without one, the top two meet again on the November ballot. The LAO's summary: the lieutenant governor "serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" in the first case and "for the rest of the term" in the second.
Because Prop 5 removes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer's candidacy, a governor recalled early in a term could appear in that special election. The same applies to a recalled legislator in the special election that would fill the seat. The only limit the text adds is on appointment: a recalled officer "shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
That provision is the one even the measure's author has not defended. Newman told the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board he could not explain why it is there: "I'm honestly not sure," he said (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php). "It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." The Yes campaign's website (https://fixtherecall.com/) presents it as a feature, saying that today's process "locks the recalled official out of the race entirely" and that under Prop 5 "the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run." That description fits legislative seats and an early-term governor recall; for a governor recalled late in a term and for other statewide offices, the text provides succession or appointment, not an election.
California recall history: 182 attempts, 11 elections, six removals since 1913
The Secretary of State counts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 57 of them against governors. Eleven qualified for the ballot: nine against legislators and two against governors. Six succeeded: Senators Marshall Black (1913) and Edwin Grant (1914), Assembly members Paul Horcher (1994) and Doris Allen (1995), Governor Gray Davis (2003) and Senator Josh Newman (2018). No state recall effort is in circulation now, according to the Secretary of State's current-efforts page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/current-recall-efforts).
The three most recent recalls show what the replacement question does. In 2003 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2003-special/sum.pdf), 55.4% voted to recall Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement contest with 4,206,284 votes, 48.6% of the votes for a candidate and more than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis. In 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-primary/sov/15-state-senator-29th-district.pdf), 58.1% voted to recall Newman in the 29th Senate District, and Republican Ling Ling Chang won the seat with 50,215 votes, 33.8% of the replacement vote and 15,982 fewer than the 66,197 cast for Newman to stay. In 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/11-sov-summary.pdf), 61.9% voted against recalling Governor Newsom; the leading replacement candidate, Larry Elder, received 3,563,867 votes, which would have made him governor with 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question had the recall passed. That is the "about 28%" figure in the Yes argument.
California recall results are showing replacement winners at 46.8% and 31.8% of the recall vote in 2003 and 2018, and 27.8% for 2021's leading candidate, in Secretary of State data compiled in October 2026. California is one of seven states that choose a successor on the same ballot as the recall, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures' survey (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials) of the 19 states that allow recall of state officials. Five others hold a separate special election and eight fill the vacancy by appointment, with some states mixing methods by office. Other reform ideas have taken different routes: the state's Little Hoover Commission recommended (https://lhc.ca.gov/press-release-43/) in 2022 a "snap" election in which "the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements," plus a statewide signature threshold of 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 adopts neither.
Prop 5's cost: Savings or costs "in the range of millions of dollars," depending on the recall
The LAO's fiscal estimate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) is "unknown," because it depends on how often recalls happen and which offices they target. Removing the second question would save money on ballots and voter materials when no follow-up election is needed, which is the case for a governor recalled late in a term and for offices filled by appointment. A legislative recall would cost more if the follow-up special election "could not be consolidated with a scheduled election," at "millions of dollars per election." The LAO puts the net effect at "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," less than 0.1% of the General Fund.
For scale, the Department of Finance's July 1, 2021 letter (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/dof-allocation-costs-letter.pdf) estimated $243.6 million for counties and $32.4 million for the Secretary of State, $276 million in all, of which the Legislature appropriated $250.2 million; the same letter estimated $90.6 million if the recall had been consolidated with a regular election. Prop 5 does not change the cost of the recall election itself, only of what follows it.
Proposition 5's author and the vote in the Legislature
Newman, a Fullerton Democrat, introduced SCA 1 in January 2023. It passed the Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024 and, after amendment, the Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; the Senate concurred 32–8 the next day, and it was filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) with the Secretary of State on September 10, 2024, directed to this November's ballot. Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of each house. The Chronicle's editorial board notes that Newman was recalled in 2018, won the seat back in 2020 and lost again in 2024. Of the 2018 recall, which his opponents tie to his vote to raise gas taxes, he told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/): "I didn't do anything other than cast a tough vote."
Nobody is spending money on the measure. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) for Prop 5 reports "No committees identified" on either side as of October 6, and no Prop 5 committee appears on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), which covers committees that have raised $1 million. The Yes campaign's website is paid for by Californians For a Prosperous Golden State, the committee listed with Newman as the ballot contact. No opposition contact is listed in the Voter Information Guide.
The arguments: Majority rule versus the voters' pick
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, says the two questions together create "a dangerous loophole": "An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast." It cites the 2021 recall's cost as "more than $200 million" and says Prop 5 would stop recalls being used "to 'redo' an election as a political or partisan scheme." The Department of Finance's figures above support the cost claim; the 28% figure matches the Statement of Vote.
The No argument, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, says Prop 5 "will take away your voice" because "politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" in many cases, and other seats "would sit vacant until another costly election." It objects that "that failed politician you just ran out the door… they'd be allowed to run in that next election," and its rebuttal says the author wants to change the rules after being recalled "when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises." Carl DeMaio, the Prop 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) proponent, told CalMatters voters could be "without a representative for months, if not longer." I'm noting that nobody is spending money on this measure, so it has no organized support or opposition. That means the result will likely follow the general mood of voters, shaped by the voter guide, party cues, the ballot label, and newspaper endorsements. I also see that both the "takes away your voice" argument against and the "majority rule" argument for feel intuitive. Next I want to look at the polling section.

I'm planning to check how the PPIC October poll's Prop 5 numbers compared to the final result, and to look at party-level crosstabs. I'd like a base rate from similar low-campaign measures in past elections, so I'm going to search for those poll figures.

I'm working through how PPIC's likely-voter numbers would map onto the final result, and I'm also planning to check how "don't know" respondents tend to split. The October poll ran after ballots had already gone out, so a large share of voters had already cast their ballots before the survey closed. The later deciders who make up the rest of the electorate may lean more partisan and less informed, and recent California patterns of late-arriving ballots could shift that mix, so I want to account for it.

I'm now checking who is behind the "No on Prop 5" side, starting with the Mercury News Q&A with its campaign. I'll also look at which other groups and editorial boards have taken positions on the measure.

Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, Secretary of State and FPPC campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026, endorsements as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 10, 2026.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

I'm recording the 2024 PPIC October poll against the actual results. Prop 3 was polled at 67% yes and came in at 62.6%, Prop 5 was polled at 48% and came in at 45.0%, and I'm now comparing Prop 6's October numbers with its actual result.

I'm checking Prop 6's two-party share in October, which was 42.3% against an actual 46.2%. Prop 2 and Prop 4 also have their actual results noted, though their poll figures are still unclear. Given typical errors of about 4 to 5 points, I'm estimating Prop 5's chance of passing from its October two-party share of 46.4%, and noting that past polls have missed in both directions.

I'm weighing how a continuing Sept-to-Oct climb might push Prop 5 higher, though Prop 6's 2024 drop from 46 to 41 still ended at 46.2, so late movement can go either way. I'm also considering whether the strongly Democratic 2026 environment lifts a measure with mostly establishment backing, since results tend to track partisan share times each party's support.

I'm estimating the electorate's partisan split for 2026, comparing it to 2024's D+20 environment. For Prop 5, I'm working through a scenario where Democrats back it at about 62%, Republicans at 28%, and independents at 42%, which gives roughly 48% yes overall.

I'm working through how late deciders might break for Prop 5. With no campaign, voters fall back on their priors and the ballot label, and many default to "No" when the wording sounds like a process change. PPIC polls also tend to push undecided respondents toward an answer, so their unsure share is probably understated, which makes me think the measure more likely fails by a few to several points.

I'm now looking for more recent data, such as early-vote figures and other forecasts, to refine the estimate. The On Point Polling model puts Prop 5 at a 45.7% chance of passing, starting from a prior of about 70% yes based on the measure's history and its legislative origin, and then pulling down toward the polling average of 43.2%. That site may be automated, so I don't fully trust it, but its blend of prior and polls is worth noting. Its 49.5% yes figure is roughly where I'd place the measure, just under the line.

I'm now wondering whether Prop 5's 2026 poll numbers are actually in line with the rest of the record, so I want to check other sources like Emerson, Citrin Center, and CalMatters for more recent figures. I'm also weighing the On Point model's 70% prior against its polling average, since that prior looks heavy for a measure polling in the mid-40s.

I'm checking the LA Times editorial board's position on Prop 5 next.

PPIC's October 2024 poll landed close to the results in both directions: Prop 5 was polled at 48% and got 45%, while Prop 6 was polled at 41% and got 46%. Next I'll look for other Prop 5 polling and for how major editorial boards and groups lined up.

# Proposition 5
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Two Questions in Recall Elections.*** In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office.
...
### Proposal
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.

# County Republicans meet, state parties chart opposing paths on Nov. 3 ballot
California’s Democratic and Republican party organizations have issued competing road maps for the Nov. 3 general election, endorsing opposing slates for statewide office and taking sharply different positions on many of the 14 propositions before voters.
The recommendations are party endorsements, not official voting instructions.
Voters may support any candidate or position regardless of registration, and the state parties generally leave city, county and other local contests to local party committees.

The California Democratic Party endorsed Xavier Becerra for governor and Fiona Ma for lieutenant governor.

For the Board of Equalization, Democrats endorsed Nelson Esparza in District 1, Sally Lieber in District 2, Mike Gipson in District 3 and Tom Umberg in District 4.
In contests affecting the Mariposa area, the party endorsed Michael Masuda in the 5th Congressional District and Jaron Brandon in the 4th State Senate District.

Let’s Fix California’s Broken Recall System Together.
Learn More
Right now, a recall election asks Californians two questions at once.
The second one is the problem: it hands the seat to whoever finishes first in a crowded field, sometimes with a sliver of the vote, and it locks the recalled official out of the race entirely.
The Solution
Proposition 5 puts the decision back where it belongs.
Recall an official, and the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run and voters choose a replacement outright. This isn’t about protecting any party or any officeholder. It’s about making sure the person who ends up in the seat actually won it.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.

Support

Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

## Proposition 5
**The basics**
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years.
In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic.
But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.

### Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
**The impact**
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.

I'm trying to calibrate against the October 2024 PPIC crosstabs for Prop 6, and I need to get the row order right: the "don't know" figures come first, then the No and Yes shares.

I'm reading the October PPIC table row by row: the No share comes out at 56% overall, and Yes at 41%. Looking at the Yes row by group, Democrats are at 56%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 38%.

I'm working out the implied electorate weights for the 2024 Prop 6 result: if Democrats came in around 65%, Republicans near 22%, and independents at 42%, the weighted total lands close to the actual 46.2% yes. I'm then carrying those same shifts over to Prop 5 for 2026 and getting a rough final figure near 50%.

I'm weighing the October PPIC figures against the September poll for Prop 6, where it stood at 46% yes versus 41% in October. Taking the September number as the more representative one, the final 46.2% fits it closely, which suggests the October reading was just noise. Averaging the two polls gives about 43.5%, and the actual result landed roughly 2.7 points above that. For Prop 5 in 2026 I'm noting the September figure at 35% and the October figure at 45%.

I'm weighing whether the October reading was just a noisy high, which would put Prop 5's final near 44%, or whether the rise reflects a real trend that could carry it to 47-49%. Other propositions in the same series also moved up between September and October, and Prop 5's jump is the largest of them, so I'm checking the September party splits for Prop 5 next.

The October jump for Democrats, from 40 to 56, looks like cue-taking after the party's endorsement and the slate mailers. Republicans moved the other way, from 34 down to 28. I'm checking whether earlier low-information measures in prior elections showed similar late swings, starting with how Prop 6 moved in 2024.

I'm checking the 2024 Prop 5 figures from the same crosstabs next: the Democratic Yes share looks like it came in around 68%, and I want to confirm that against the other rows before comparing it to the October reading.

I'm checking the Prop 5 Yes row from the October 2024 table, where Democrats come in at 68%, Republicans at 15%, and independents at 43%, for an overall total of 48% against the actual 45%. That suggests the Democratic share in that poll ran high relative to the final result, so I'm guessing Prop 6's Democratic figure could have shifted up as well.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024: both Democratic-backed measures finished near 45-46% despite polls showing 48 and 41. That suggests the final Yes share for a similar 2026 measure would land around 47-48%, and getting past 50% would need unusually strong consolidation.

I'm weighing the Prop 6 and Prop 5 outcomes from 2024 against the broader electorate: both Democratic-backed measures landed in the mid-40s despite polling higher, so I'm reconsidering whether the Democratic environment in 2026 really adds enough to push a low-salience measure past 50%.

I'm checking the 2026 Prop 5 electorate estimate: the Dem-margin figure is around D+22 to D+25, and I'm running a rough regression off the 2024 Prop 5 and Prop 6 results, which both landed near 45-46%. Projecting that forward gives a final around 46-47%, so I'd put the chance of Yes clearing 50% at roughly 15-20%.

I'm weighing whether the Democratic slate language, which frames the measure as protecting the right to recall, would hold up as well as the 2024 "slavery" wording did, since that one still lost with Democrats and independents peeling off over the confusion. Overall I'd lean toward the lower-salience, GOP-opposed pattern holding, so Yes staying under 50% still looks like the more likely outcome.

Next I want to confirm the outcome isn't already known by checking for early returns on the Prop 5 recall, since the latest coverage I've seen stops at Nov 2.

I'm going to search for the Prop 5 results and election night race calls, to see whether the outcome is already reported.

The 2024 Prop 6 had nearly the same party split as Prop 5 now, and it finished at 46.2%, so Democratic-backed low-salience amendments have tended to land in the mid-40s. I'm running one last check for any election-night results.
